title: Reimagining social protection: financialised futures among ageing migrant domestic workers in Asia
venue: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies
tldr: Ageing Filipino migrant domestic workers in Singapore and Hong Kong increasingly enrol in financial literacy courses, generating new financialised aspirations while alternative social protection strategies persist alongside.
problem_and_motivation: Ageing Filipino migrant domestic workers on restrictive temporary work visas in Singapore and Hong Kong face mandatory retirement and return to the Philippines with limited state-based social protection and uncertain kinship care. A growing landscape of financial education courses promoted by state, corporate, and NGO actors has emerged to address this gap, yet little is known about how these women engage with financialisation as a social protection strategy and how it interacts with existing interdependencies.
approach: Ethnographic research conducted between 2018 and 2022 with middle-aged and older migrant domestic workers in Singapore and Hong Kong.
Over 50 in-depth interviews with domestic workers of different nationalities, policy officers, co-operative and NGO representatives.
Observations in three organisations offering financial education courses, including NGO-run classes, co-operative-led sessions, and corporate-sponsored seminars.
Individual life-story interviews and focus group discussions with 20 women participating in financial education courses, plus non-participants.
Online observation of financial education organisations during COVID-19 pandemic including livestreamed classes, webinars, and social media.
Narrative analysis of migration trajectories from breadwinner mentality to financialised self-reliance, including identification of counter-narratives.
Analysis of diverse financial education offerings ranging from basic saving and budgeting to corporate investment seminars and cooperative models.
findings: num: Only 5% of overseas Filipinos in Singapore had been paying into the Philippine Social Security System (SSS).
One NGO estimates close to 15,000 domestic workers in its community with over 8,000 course graduates in 2018.
Another organisation reports 70,000 programme participants since its founding in the late 2000s.
Financial education courses attract predominantly Filipino domestic workers, followed by Indonesians, with few from other nationalities.
Financialisation does not represent a complete rupture with kinship obligations but generates more subtle shifts and new conversations about money management.

definitions.definition: The increasing role of financial motives, markets, actors, and institutions in the operation of the economy and its governance applied to social protection.
Formal and informal welfare mechanisms migrants navigate across national borders combining state, kinship, and market-based resources.
The Philippine state's contributory pension system offering coverage for illness, disability, housing loans, healthcare, and pensions for overseas Filipino workers.
A Philippine state entity partnering with SSS for housing loan provisions to overseas Filipino workers.
The Philippine state entity partnering with SSS for healthcare coverage of overseas Filipino workers.
Overseas Filipino Worker, a Philippine government designation for Filipino nationals working abroad under temporary migration contracts.
A category of Philippine diaspora typically holding long-term residence or citizenship abroad who return to visit the Philippines.
Filipino village-based informal lending circles in which migrant women participate for saving or borrowing for immediate needs.
Money sent by migrant workers to their families in their countries of origin, a central component of transnational family support.
The Philippine state's highly institutionalised system of facilitating overseas employment of Filipino workers, in force since the 1970s.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes to scholarship on transnational social protection by documenting how financialisation emerges as an alternative or supplement to state and kinship-based welfare for ageing migrant domestic workers. It provides ethnographic evidence of how financial education courses generate new self-oriented financial aspirations among Filipino women approaching retirement abroad. The paper demonstrates that financialisation does not produce a clean rupture with kinship obligations but rather creates reconfigured interdependencies among migrants, kin, employers, and the state. It further contributes by documenting counter-narratives including political activism, faith-based approaches, and traditional land-based strategies that exist alongside financialised modes of thinking about future security.
directly_justifies: Only 5% of overseas Filipinos in Singapore had been paying into the Philippine Social Security System.
Financial education courses generate new financialised aspirations revolving around self-responsibility for success and security in later life.
Financialisation does not represent a complete rupture with kinship obligations but generates more subtle shifts in migrant women's money management.
Migrant women's social protection strategies are increasingly complex and diverse, with financialisation becoming one visible option in the landscape.
An NGO estimates close to 15,000 domestic workers in its community with over 8,000 course graduates in 2018.
limits: Ethnographic methodology limits generalisability across all migrant domestic worker communities in Asia.
Focus on Filipino workers, though brief mention of Indonesian, Indian, and Sri Lankan workers, limits comparative analysis of nationality-specific financialisation patterns.
No systematic measurement of financialisation's extent among the wider domestic worker community beyond those observed in courses.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned for relevance. Domain 1 (Filipino Young Professionals as a Demographic) was flagged as medium relevance because the paper focuses on older Filipino migrant domestic workers rather than young professionals specifically, though demographic and financial characteristics are explored. Domain 2 (Financial Structure, Behavior, and Culturally Specific Practices) was flagged as high relevance for 2.A and 2.C, with 2.D at medium, because the paper directly examines paluwagan lending circles, remittance obligations, and migrants' self-declared financial preferences. Domain 3 (Expense Categorization) was considered and rejected as the paper does not propose or evaluate expense categorization frameworks. Domain 4 (Existing Personal Finance Systems) was flagged low because while the paper describes financial education offerings, it does not evaluate software-based personal finance systems. Domain 5 (Financial Behavioral Profiles) was considered but the paper does not develop or evaluate behavioral profiling approaches. Domain 6 (Predictive Modeling) was rejected as the paper is purely qualitative. Domain 7 (Budgeting Strategies) was flagged medium for 7.A as the paper discusses budgeting education but does not involve algorithmic recommendation. Domain 8 (Anomaly Detection) was rejected as irrelevant. Domain 9 (Mobile-First Design) was rejected. Domain 10 (Data Privacy and Security) was flagged contextual for 10.A due to scam identification teachings. Domain 11 (Engagement Dynamics) was flagged medium for 11.A because the paper analyzes motivation and peer-driven engagement with financial courses. Domain 12 (Evaluation Frameworks) was flagged low for 12.A as the paper offers ethnographic assessment rather than systematic evaluation. Domains 13 (Savings Goal and Debt Management) and 14 (Synthetic Data Generation) were considered and rejected. Overall, the paper's topical coverage centers on Filipino migrant demographic characteristics, financial behavior and culturally specific practices, with peripheral relevance to financial education engagement and budgeting knowledge.

limitations: Methodology is purely ethnographic with no quantitative measures of financialisation outcomes or cost-effectiveness of financial education courses. [unacknowledged]
Sample may be self-selecting as course participants were willing to be interviewed, potentially excluding non-participants who could offer different perspectives. [unacknowledged]
The paper does not systematically measure the long-term financial outcomes of course participation for returned migrants.
Fieldwork was interrupted by COVID-19 pandemic between 2020 and 2022, potentially affecting observation continuity.
remember_this: Ageing Filipino migrant domestic workers face mandatory retirement with limited state-based social protection and uncertain kinship care.
Financial education courses promote self-responsibility and individualised financial strategies as alternatives to relying on kin or the state.
Only 5% of overseas Filipinos in Singapore had been contributing to the Philippine Social Security System.
Financialisation does not replace social relationships but reconfigures interdependencies between migrants, kin, employers, and the state.
Counter-narratives including political activism, faith-based living, and land-based strategies persist alongside financialised approaches.
